name: Government Budget Balance
expression: Budget balance = Revenue (net of transfer payments) − Expenditure (including debt-interest payments)
meaning: Measures whether a government ran a surplus or a deficit over a fiscal period.

variables.Revenue: tax revenue net of transfer payments
variables.Expenditure: total government spending, including debt-interest payments

intuition: A positive balance means the government collected more than it spent; a negative balance means it had to borrow to cover the shortfall.
workedExample: Revenue of 769 billion and expenditure of 808 billion give a balance of −39 billion, a deficit.
commonMistake: Reversing the subtraction order and misreading a deficit as a surplus.
relatedLearningOutcome: describe roles and objectives of fiscal policy as well as arguments as to whether the size of a national debt relative to GDP matters

name: Disposable Income
meaning: Income remaining after net taxes, available to be spent or saved.

variables.t: net tax rate, assumed proportional to income

intuition: Only the after-tax portion of income is available for households to spend or save.
workedExample: If income rises by 500 million and t=20%, disposable income rises by 400 million.
commonMistake: Applying the tax rate to the wrong base, such as disposable income itself instead of the change in national income.
relatedLearningOutcome: describe tools of fiscal policy, including their advantages and disadvantages

name: MPC and MPS Identity
meaning: The marginal propensity to consume and the marginal propensity to save out of an additional unit of disposable income must sum to one.
intuition: Every additional unit of disposable income is either spent or saved; there is no third option.
workedExample: Disposable income of 80 with consumption of 72 gives MPC=72/80=0.9 and MPS=1−0.9=0.1.
commonMistake: Computing MPC using pre-tax income instead of disposable income.
relatedLearningOutcome: describe tools of fiscal policy, including their advantages and disadvantages

name: Simple (No-Tax) Multiplier
meaning: The total output effect of a change in autonomous spending when there is no tax leakage.
intuition: Each round of new spending becomes someone else's income, part of which is spent again; summing every round gives the multiplier.
workedExample: MPC=0.9 gives a simple multiplier of 1/(1−0.9)=10.
commonMistake: Estimating the multiplier by eye for MPC values close to 1, where small changes have a large nonlinear effect.
relatedLearningOutcome: describe tools of fiscal policy, including their advantages and disadvantages

name: Fiscal Multiplier
meaning: The total output effect of a change in government spending or autonomous demand when a proportional tax rate is in place.
intuition: A tax rate reduces the effective spending ratio each round to c(1−t), shrinking the multiplier relative to the no-tax case; setting t=0 recovers the simple multiplier.
workedExample: c=0.9 and t=20% give a fiscal multiplier of 1/[1−0.9(0.8)]=1/0.28≈3.57, so a 1 billion rise in spending raises income by about 3.57 billion.
commonMistake: Subtracting t from c directly instead of computing c(1−t) first.
relatedLearningOutcome: describe tools of fiscal policy, including their advantages and disadvantages

name: Balanced Budget Multiplier
expression: If ΔG = ΔT, the balanced budget multiplier ΔY/ΔG always equals 1
meaning: An equal increase in government spending and taxes still raises equilibrium output, by exactly the size of the increase.

variables.ΔT: change in taxes (equal to ΔG in the balanced case)

intuition: The direct spending injection (ΔG) is only partly offset by the reduction in consumption from the tax rise (c×ΔT), leaving a positive net injection that compounds through the ordinary multiplier back up to exactly ΔG.
workedExample: ΔG=ΔT=200 million and c=0.9: net initial impact is 200−0.9(200)=20 million, which compounds via the simple multiplier (10) to a total effect of 200 million, equal to ΔG.
commonMistake: Assuming a balanced budget has no effect on output because taxes rose by the same amount as spending.
relatedLearningOutcome: describe tools of fiscal policy, including their advantages and disadvantages

name: Government Debt-to-GDP Ratio
expression: Debt-to-GDP ratio = Total outstanding government debt / Nominal GDP
meaning: Scales the stock of government debt by the size of the economy that ultimately services it; the central measure debated in the arguments for and against debt concern.

variables.Total outstanding government debt: cumulative stock of past deficits financed by borrowing
variables.Nominal GDP: gross domestic product at current prices

intuition: The ratio tends to worsen when the real interest rate on the debt exceeds the real growth rate of the economy, since the debt burden then compounds faster than the tax base that services it.
workedExample: Government debt of 1.4 trillion against GDP of 2.0 trillion gives a debt-to-GDP ratio of 70%.
commonMistake: Treating the absolute level of debt as informative on its own, without scaling by the size of the economy or comparing the real interest rate with real growth.
relatedLearningOutcome: describe roles and objectives of fiscal policy as well as arguments as to whether the size of a national debt relative to GDP matters
